claim: High-frequency activity (HFA) is modulated by the phase of low-frequency activity.
source: Prior studies have shown that high-frequency activity (HFA) is modulated by the phase of low-frequency activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by references to prior studies, indicating citation-based evidence.

claim: Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) is often interpreted as reflecting phase coding of neural representations.
source: This phenomenon of phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) is often interpreted as reflecting phase coding of neural representations, although evidence for this link is still lacking in humans.
evidence: The claim is based on established interpretations in the field, representing scientific knowledge.

claim: Evidence for the link between PAC and phase coding is still lacking in humans.
source: This phenomenon of phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) is often interpreted as reflecting phase coding of neural representations, although evidence for this link is still lacking in humans.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: PAC was observed at 43% of electrodes.
source: Analyzing 167 electrodes, we observed PAC at 43% of electrodes.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Category specific HFA modulations occurred at different phases and frequencies of the underlying low-frequency rhythm.
source: Further inspection of PAC revealed that category specific HFA modulations occurred at different phases and frequencies of the underlying low-frequency rhythm, permitting decoding of categorical information using the phase at which HFA events occurred.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from the study.

claim: Categorical information can be decoded using the phase at which HFA events occurred.
source: Further inspection of PAC revealed that category specific HFA modulations occurred at different phases and frequencies of the underlying low-frequency rhythm, permitting decoding of categorical information using the phase at which HFA events occurred.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing successful decoding.

claim: PAC coincides with phase-dependent coding in the human brain.
source: These results provide evidence for categorical phase-coded neural representations and are the first to show that PAC coincides with phase-dependent coding in the human brain.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Human neuronal firing carries information about perceptual and mnemonic representations.
source: Human neuronal firing (Ekstrom et al., 2007; Kraskov et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2011; Rey et al., 2014) and increases in high-frequency activity (HFA) in the gamma range (above 30 Hz; Jacobs and Kahana, 2009; Jacobs et al., 2012; van Gerven et al., 2013) carry information about perceptual and mnemonic representations.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Increases in high-frequency activity (HFA) in the gamma range (above 30 Hz) carry information about perceptual and mnemonic representations.
source: Human neuronal firing (Ekstrom et al., 2007; Kraskov et al., 2007; Chan et al., 2011; Rey et al., 2014) and increases in high-frequency activity (HFA) in the gamma range (above 30 Hz; Jacobs and Kahana, 2009; Jacobs et al., 2012; van Gerven et al., 2013) carry information about perceptual and mnemonic representations.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Neuronal firing and HFA are positively correlated.
source: Several recent studies have shown that these two signals are positively correlated (Ray et al., 2008; Manning et al., 2009; Whittingstall and Logothetis, 2009; Miller et al., 2014; Rey et al., 2014; Burke et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Neuronal firing and HFA are each modulated by the phase of low frequency oscillations.
source: Several recent studies have shown that these two signals are positively correlated (Ray et al., 2008; Manning et al., 2009; Whittingstall and Logothetis, 2009; Miller et al., 2014; Rey et al., 2014; Burke et al., 2015) and are each modulated by the phase of low frequency oscillations (LFO) (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Bragin et al., 1995; Skaggs et al., 1996; Canolty et al., 2006; Jacobs et al., 2007; Tort et al., 2009; Axmacher et al., 2010; Rutishauser et al., 2010; McGinn and Valiante, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Phase modulation is detectable as phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) of gamma amplitude to LFO phase.
source: This modulation is detectable as phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) of gamma amplitude to LFO phase (Buzsaki, 2010; Miller et al., 2014; Aru et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: LFO phase may organize cell assemblies.
source: Together, these findings have motivated models positing that LFO phase may organize cell assemblies (Kayser et al., 2012; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Jensen et al., 2014; Watrous et al., 2015), a form of phase coding (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993).
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical models cited from prior research.

claim: LFO phase can be used to decode behaviorally relevant information.
source: Supporting this view, LFO phase can be used to decode behaviorally relevant information (Belitski et al., 2008, 2010; Fell et al., 2008; Schyns et al., 2011; Lopour et al., 2013; Ng et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Phase coded neural activity has been demonstrated in rodents.
source: phase coded neural activity has been demonstrated in rodents (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Skaggs et al., 1996) and monkeys (Kayser et al., 2009; Siegel et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Phase coded neural activity has been demonstrated in monkeys.
source: phase coded neural activity has been demonstrated in rodents (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Skaggs et al., 1996) and monkeys (Kayser et al., 2009; Siegel et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PAC observed in humans has been thought to reflect phase-coding.
source: Although the PAC observed in humans (Canolty et al., 2006; Axmacher et al., 2010) has been thought to reflect phase-coding, this assumption has yet to be validated because prior studies have not investigated the relation between PAC and decoding from LFO phases.
evidence: The claim is based on prior interpretations in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Prior studies have not investigated the relation between PAC and decoding from LFO phases.
source: Although the PAC observed in humans (Canolty et al., 2006; Axmacher et al., 2010) has been thought to reflect phase-coding, this assumption has yet to be validated because prior studies have not investigated the relation between PAC and decoding from LFO phases.
evidence: The claim is based on the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: The frequency-specific phase of LFO coordinates neural firing to support neural representations.
source: We have recently proposed that the frequency-specific phase of LFO coordinates neural firing to support neural representations (Watrous and Ekstrom, 2014; Watrous et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on a theoretical proposal by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Data were analyzed from 167 intracranially-recorded EEG electrodes from six patients with pharmaco-resistant epilepsy.
source: We analyzed data from a total of 167 intracranially-recorded EEG electrodes from six patients with pharmaco-resistant epilepsy as they viewed pictures of houses, faces, tools, and outdoor scenes
evidence: The claim describes the experimental setup and data collection.

claim: At least 20% of electrodes in each patient showed significant PAC.
source: We found robust evidence for PAC, with at least 20% of electrodes in each patient showing significant PAC (n = 72/167 'PAC+' electrodes, see 'Materials and methods' for statistical assessment and inclusion criteria).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: 72 out of 167 electrodes showed significant PAC.
source: We found robust evidence for PAC, with at least 20% of electrodes in each patient showing significant PAC (n = 72/167 'PAC+' electrodes, see 'Materials and methods' for statistical assessment and inclusion criteria).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: HFA increased approximately 150 ms after stimulus onset.
source: HFA was broadly distributed across trials and time points. Calculating the proportion of trials showing a period of significantly increased HFA (95th percentile, see 'Materials and methods' for 'HFA windows') on each PAC+ electrode and category, we found that HFA occurred throughout the period of stimulus presentation but increased ∼150 ms after stimulus onset (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 2F.

claim: 66% of trials had at least one HFA window.
source: 66% of trials had at least one HFA window and this prevalence did not vary by category (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; one-way ANOVA, F(3,284) = 0.6, p > 0.61).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The prevalence of HFA windows did not vary by category.
source: 66% of trials had at least one HFA window and this prevalence did not vary by category (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; one-way ANOVA, F(3,284) = 0.6, p > 0.61).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of experimental data.

claim: Slow-modulating frequencies were significantly clustered in the delta band (0.5–4 Hz).
source: Slow-modulating ('Fphase') frequencies were significantly clustered in the delta band (0.5–4 Hz; Figure 2G)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 2G.

claim: HFA modulated frequencies were significantly clustered around slow (∼32 Hz) and fast (∼110 Hz) gamma frequencies.
source: HFA modulated frequencies ('Famp') were significantly clustered around slow (∼32 Hz) and fast (∼110 Hz) gamma frequencies (Figure 2H, chi-square goodness of fit test across gamma frequencies, p < 0.004, χ2(22) = 43.6, Cohen's d = 0.77).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (chi-square test).

claim: HFA was typically maximal near the trough of the oscillation (at 180°).
source: Furthermore, we found that HFA was typically maximal near the trough of the oscillation (i.e., at 180°; Figure 2I; p < 0.05, Rayleigh test; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for additional examples and modulation at other phases).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (Rayleigh test).

claim: 87% (63/72) of PAC+ electrodes showed significant clustering for all four categories.
source: This analysis revealed significant clustering for all four categories on 87% (63/72) of PAC+ electrodes (Rayleigh test p < 0.00004, Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01 for PAC+ electrodes and categories).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (Rayleigh test).

claim: Phase clustering was observed in each patient.
source: Phase clustering was observed in each patient and did not vary across categories at FMAX (one-way ANOVA on resultant vector lengths, F(3,284) = 0.14, p > 0.93).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (ANOVA).

claim: Phase clustering did not vary across categories at FMAX.
source: Phase clustering was observed in each patient and did not vary across categories at FMAX (one-way ANOVA on resultant vector lengths, F(3,284) = 0.14, p > 0.93).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of experimental data.

claim: 78% (49/63) of PAC+ electrodes showed a unique phase-clustering profile for one category compared with each other category.
source: Across all patients, 78% (49/63) of PAC+ electrodes showed a unique phase-clustering profile for one category compared with each other category (e.g., Figure 1B; DS = 3 for at least one category, p < 10−9, Watson Williams test, Bonferroni corrected across comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (Watson Williams test).

claim: At least 15% of electrodes in each patient showed unique phase-clustering profiles.
source: This pattern was consistent both within and across patients, with at least 15% of electrodes in each patient showing these effects (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Categories with larger DSs exhibited larger phase differences with other categories.
source: We next calculated the average phase difference between categories, expecting this measure to increase with increasing DS. Indeed, categories with larger DSs exhibited larger phase differences with other categories such that maximally distinct representations were 35° phase offset from all other categories (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Maximally distinct representations were 35° phase offset from all other categories.
source: Indeed, categories with larger DSs exhibited larger phase differences with other categories such that maximally distinct representations were 35° phase offset from all other categories (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Phase-coding was equally likely to occur at all phases across electrodes.
source: In fact, across electrodes, phase-coding was equally likely to occur at all phases and for all categories; phase-coded categories were not clustered at particular phases at any level of DS (Rayleigh test, all p > 0.19; Figure 3F)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Rayleigh test) of experimental data.

claim: Phase-coding was equally likely for each category.
source: phase-coding was equally likely for each category (χ2(3) = 1.6, p = 0.64).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (chi-square test) of experimental data.

claim: 42 (25% of all) electrodes showed significant decoding accuracy compared to category label shuffled surrogates.
source: As expected from the analysis using DS, 42 (25% of all) electrodes showed significant decoding accuracy (using LFO phases during HFA windows as features) compared to category label shuffled surrogates and this proportion was significantly higher than would be expected by chance (p < 10−10, binomial test, chance level: 8.3 electrodes, Cohen's d = 0.6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (binomial test).

claim: 19 (11%) electrodes showed significantly higher decoding accuracy during HFA events as compared to random event surrogates.
source: 19 (11%) electrodes showed significantly higher decoding accuracy during HFA events as compared to random event surrogates, and this proportion was significantly higher than would be expected by chance (p < 0.0003, binomial test, chance = 8.3 electrodes, Cohen's d = 0.22).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (binomial test).

claim: 17 (10%) electrodes showed significant enhancements of decoding accuracy during HFA events relative to both label and event shuffled surrogates.
source: Moreover, 17 (10%) electrodes showed significant enhancements of decoding accuracy during HFA events relative to both label and event shuffled surrogates, with at least two electrodes in each patient showing this pattern. This proportion of electrodes far exceeded that expected by chance (p < 10−10, binomial test, chance = 0.41 electrodes, Cohen's d = 0.46).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (binomial test).

claim: At least two electrodes in each patient showed significant enhancements of decoding accuracy during HFA events relative to both label and event shuffled surrogates.
source: Moreover, 17 (10%) electrodes showed significant enhancements of decoding accuracy during HFA events relative to both label and event shuffled surrogates, with at least two electrodes in each patient showing this pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Phase clustering was larger at FMAX compared to at FMIN on PAC+ electrodes.
source: As one would expect, on PAC+ electrodes, phase clustering was larger at FMAX compared to at FMIN, both on individual electrodes (Figure 4A, B) and at the group level (Figure 4C; paired t-test on resultant vector lengths, t(287) = 8, p < 10−10, Cohen's d = 0.32).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis (paired t-test).

claim: Only 20% (15/72) of PAC+ electrodes showed significant phase-clustering at FMIN for all 4 categories.
source: Moreover, only 20% (15/72) of PAC+ electrodes showed significant phase-clustering at FMIN for all 4 categories and only 1 electrode showed category-selective phase-clustering of HFA events.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Only 1 electrode showed category-selective phase-clustering of HFA events at FMIN.
source: Moreover, only 20% (15/72) of PAC+ electrodes showed significant phase-clustering at FMIN for all 4 categories and only 1 electrode showed category-selective phase-clustering of HFA events.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Enhanced phase-clustering was found around 0.5 and 1 Hz across the full range of frequencies (1–12 Hz).
source: We therefore recalculated phase clustering across the full range of frequencies (1–12 Hz, 0.1 Hz steps). Again, we found enhanced phase-clustering around 0.5 and 1 Hz (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), but not at adjacent frequencies as would be expected from this alternative account.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: HFA at distinct phases and frequencies reflect representations for different categories.
source: Taken together, these results support the conclusion that HFA at distinct phases and frequencies reflect representations for different categories.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Phase-coding of categorical information extended beyond brain areas associated with higher-order vision.
source: Intriguingly, phase-coding of categorical information extended beyond brain areas associated with higher-order vision.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations from the study.

claim: Category-specificity does not appear to exclusively relate to perception but may also involve other more complex, and idiosyncratic, associations to these stimuli.
source: Thus, our findings of category-specificity do not appear to exclusively relate to perception but may also involve other more complex, and idiosyncratic, associations to these stimuli.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the experimental findings, involving speculation about the nature of the representations.

claim: The findings are in line with prior work which has found spatially-distributed content-specific representations.
source: Our findings are nonetheless in line with prior work (Majima et al., 2014; Yaffe et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015) which has found spatially-distributed content-specific representations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Frequency-specific PRs were identified in humans.
source: We identified frequency-specific PRs in humans, consistent with a growing body of evidence implicating the relevance of frequency-specific oscillatory activity to human cognition (Daitch et al., 2013; Watrous et al., 2013; Fontolan et al., 2014; Freudenburg et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study and citations to prior research.

claim: PAC predominantly occurs with modulating frequencies in the delta band, particularly around 1 Hz.
source: It has recently been shown that the frequency of LFOs contributes to several neuronal properties such that relatively slower LFOs lead to decreased firing threshold and increased spike timing variability (Cohen, 2014). It is not immediately clear how this relates to our finding that PAC predominantly occurs with modulating frequencies in the delta band, particularly around 1 Hz.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The timing of the task (1 image per second with a jittered inter-stimulus interval) may have partially entrained slow oscillations forming an oscillatory hierarchy.
source: A third possibility, more likely in our view based on our results indicating multiple modulating frequencies per electrode (Figure 2G), is that the timing of our task (1 image per second with a jittered inter-stimulus interval) partially entrained slow oscillations forming an oscillatory hierarchy (Lakatos et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by citation.

claim: PAC at a variety of phases and frequencies, particularly near 32 Hz, might reflect a form of 'nested coupling' distinct from 'broadband' high gamma.
source: Similarly, our results showing PAC at a variety of phases and frequencies (Maris et al., 2011; van der Meij et al., 2012), particularly near 32 Hz, might reflect a form of 'nested coupling' (Kopell et al., 2010) distinct from 'broadband' high gamma, which has been suggested to reflect population spiking (Manning et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings, supported by citations.

claim: Broadband high gamma has been suggested to reflect population spiking.
source: Similarly, our results showing PAC at a variety of phases and frequencies (Maris et al., 2011; van der Meij et al., 2012), particularly near 32 Hz, might reflect a form of 'nested coupling' (Kopell et al., 2010) distinct from 'broadband' high gamma, which has been suggested to reflect population spiking (Manning et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The results employing direct brain recordings explicitly link phase-coupled neural activity to phase coding in humans.
source: To summarize, by identifying electrodes exhibiting both PAC and phase-coded neural representations for categories, our results employing direct brain recordings explicitly link phase-coupled neural activity to phase coding in humans.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Six right handed patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy participated in the study.
source: Six right handed patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy (mean age 31.8 years; 3 female) participated in the study.
evidence: The claim describes the study participants.

claim: The mean age of patients was 31.8 years.
source: Six right handed patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy (mean age 31.8 years; 3 female) participated in the study.
evidence: The claim describes the study participants.

claim: Three patients were female.
source: Six right handed patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy (mean age 31.8 years; 3 female) participated in the study.
evidence: The claim describes the study participants.

claim: All patients were stereotactically implanted for diagnostic purposes.
source: All patients were stereotactically implanted for diagnostic purposes.
evidence: The claim describes the clinical procedure for the patients.

claim: Recordings were performed using a Stellate recording system at the Department of Epileptology, University of Bonn, Germany.
source: Recordings were performed using a Stellate recording system (Stellate GmbH, Munich, Germany) at the Department of Epileptology, University of Bonn, Germany.
evidence: The claim describes the recording equipment and location.

claim: The study was conducted according to the latest version of the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: The study was conducted according to the latest version of the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the ethical committee of the medical faculty at the University of Bonn (approval identifier 280/08).
evidence: The claim describes the ethical standards followed in the study.

claim: The study was approved by the ethical committee of the medical faculty at the University of Bonn (approval identifier 280/08).
source: The study was conducted according to the latest version of the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the ethical committee of the medical faculty at the University of Bonn (approval identifier 280/08).
evidence: The claim describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: All patients provided written informed consent to participate in the study and for the results to be published in a pseudonymized manner.
source: All patients provided written informed consent to participate in the study and for the results to be published in a pseudonymized manner.
evidence: The claim describes the informed consent process.

claim: Patients viewed greyscale images taken from four different categories (houses, tools, scenes, and faces).
source: Patients viewed greyscale images taken from four different categories (houses, tools, scenes, and faces) and each category had four unique stimuli, resulting in a stimulus set of 16 unique images.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental stimuli.

claim: Each category had four unique stimuli, resulting in a stimulus set of 16 unique images.
source: Patients viewed greyscale images taken from four different categories (houses, tools, scenes, and faces) and each category had four unique stimuli, resulting in a stimulus set of 16 unique images.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental stimuli.

claim: Each image was presented 30 times in pseudo random order (total of 480 trials).
source: Each image was presented 30 times in pseudo random order (total of 480 trials) and was followed by a white square in a fixed location.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Each image was presented for 1 s, followed by the white square presented for 1 s, and finally a jittered inter-stimulus interval ranging from 1800–2200 ms.
source: Each image was presented for 1 s, followed by the white square presented for 1 s, and finally a jittered inter-stimulus interval ranging from 1800–2200 ms.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental timing.

claim: Intracranial EEG recordings were sampled at 1000 Hz.
source: Intracranial EEG recordings (sampled at 1000 Hz) were referenced to linked mastoids and band-pass filtered (0.01 Hz [6 dB/octave] to 300 Hz [12 dB/octave]).
evidence: The claim describes the recording parameters.

claim: Intracranial EEG recordings were referenced to linked mastoids.
source: Intracranial EEG recordings (sampled at 1000 Hz) were referenced to linked mastoids and band-pass filtered (0.01 Hz [6 dB/octave] to 300 Hz [12 dB/octave]).
evidence: The claim describes the recording parameters.

claim: Intracranial EEG recordings were band-pass filtered (0.01 Hz [6 dB/octave] to 300 Hz [12 dB/octave]).
source: Intracranial EEG recordings (sampled at 1000 Hz) were referenced to linked mastoids and band-pass filtered (0.01 Hz [6 dB/octave] to 300 Hz [12 dB/octave]).
evidence: The claim describes the recording parameters.

claim: Recordings from the hemisphere contralateral to the epileptogenic focus were analyzed.
source: Recordings from the hemisphere contralateral to the epileptogenic focus were analyzed.
evidence: The claim describes the data selection criteria.

claim: An additional 32 electrodes from an ipsilateral left lateral temporal grid were included from patient 5.
source: To boost our electrode sampling, an additional 32 electrodes from an ipsilateral left lateral temporal grid were included from patient 5 based on the physicians' report, which indicated a left hippocampal focus and no evidence of neocortical lesion based on an magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
evidence: The claim describes the data inclusion criteria.

claim: Qualitatively similar results were observed when excluding the 32 ipsilateral electrodes from patient 5 from the analysis.
source: Qualitatively similar results were observed when excluding these electrodes from the analysis, with the proportions of electrodes showing any reported effect changing by no more than 3%.
evidence: The claim is supported by a control analysis performed in the study.

claim: EEG trials with artifacts (e.g., epileptiform spikes) were excluded from further analysis (15% of all trials on average).
source: EEG trials were visually inspected for artifacts (e.g., epileptiform spikes), and trials with artifacts were excluded from further analysis (15% of all trials on average).
evidence: The claim describes the data preprocessing procedure.

claim: An average of 103 trials per category and subject were analyzed.
source: We analyzed an average of 103 trials per category and subject and there were no differences in total number of trials analyzed across categories (F(3,20) = 0.38, p = 0.76).
evidence: The claim describes the data analyzed in the study.

claim: There were no differences in total number of trials analyzed across categories.
source: We analyzed an average of 103 trials per category and subject and there were no differences in total number of trials analyzed across categories (F(3,20) = 0.38, p = 0.76).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of the data.

claim: PAC was detected using the methods described by Dvorak and Fenton (2014).
source: PAC was detected using the methods described by Dvorak and Fenton (2014).
evidence: The claim describes the analysis method used, supported by citation.

claim: The OTC method is conceptually similar to an event-locked analysis around periods of enhanced HFA.
source: This method is conceptually similar to an event-locked analysis around periods of enhanced HFA.
evidence: The claim describes the conceptual basis of the analysis method.

claim: 56% (94/167) of electrodes showed PR that was larger during HFA windows compared to both time-shifted surrogates and non-HFA windows for at least one category.
source: Testing the specificity of HFA windows for phase coding, we found that 56% (94/167) of electrodes showed PR that was larger during HFA windows compared to both time-shifted surrogates and non-HFA windows for at least one category.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from a control analysis.

claim: PR values were significantly larger on PAC+ electrodes compared to electrodes without significant PAC.
source: Moreover, PR values were significantly larger on PAC+ electrodes compared to electrodes without significant PAC (two-sample t-test, p < 0.000005).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test) of experimental data.

claim: 102/167 electrodes exhibited significant PAC with delta band phase using the MI based metric.
source: Based on the MI based metric, we found that 102/167 electrodes exhibited significant PAC with delta band phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from a control analysis using an alternative method.

claim: PAC was most prominent in the delta band using MI methods.
source: Consistent with our primary results, PAC was most prominent in the delta band using these methods.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from a control analysis using an alternative method.

claim: The magnitude of gamma band activity was maximal at a similar phase of delta oscillations (180°, oscillatory trough) as when assessed using the OTC method.
source: Furthermore, the magnitude of gamma band activity was maximal at a similar phase of delta oscillations (180°, oscillatory trough) as when assessed using the OTC method.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from a control analysis using an alternative method.
